court: Nassau County District Court, First District
holding_summary: Where property is held by spouses as tenants by the entirety, one tenant may lease her interest to another without the other's consent; the non-consenting co-tenant who is himself already in possession has no exclusive right against the lessee and the eviction proceeding must be dismissed.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: The Appellate Division reversed and reinstated the Zoning Board of Appeals' determination that petitioner's leased cottage, a second dwelling on his residential lot, did not qualify as a legal preexisting nonconforming use, because the Board's finding that it was not a lawful rooming or boarding house (limited under the 1942 ordinance to no more than three boarders) was not arbitrary and capricious.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Division
holding_summary: The Appellate Division affirmed summary judgment for condominium owners, holding that a homeowners association's 2014 rules restricting short-term leasing of individual units (e.g., a two-week minimum rental period and fees) conflicted with bylaws expressly granting owners the right to lease their homes free of any restrictions, and that the board exceeded its authority by imposing such rules without a bylaw amendment.

quotes.text: “[a]ny [h]ome may be conveyed or leased by its . . . [o]wner free of any restrictions”

the plain and unequivocal provisions of the bylaws relative to the rental of individual homeowner units precludes respondents — specifically, the HOA board of directors — from unilaterally adopting the 2014 rules in the fashion accomplished here.

court: New York Supreme Court, Appellate Term
holding_summary: The Appellate Term affirmed dismissal of licensee holdover proceedings against occupants of a single-room-occupancy facility who had been referred by a city social-services agency, holding that because each occupant had continuously resided in his unit for more than six months, he qualified as a 'permanent tenant' under the Rent Stabilization Code rather than a transient licensee, defeating the operator's argument that the SRO was exempt from rent regulation as transient occupancy.

quotes.text: Respondents have conclusively established that they are not licensees, but “permanent tenant[s]” under Rent Stabilization Code (RSC) (9 NYCRR) § 2520.6 (j), since petitioner placed each respondent in occupancy of his respective SRO unit and each respondent “continuously resided” in said unit for more than six months

Respondents have conclusively established that they are not licensees, but “permanent tenant[s]” under Rent Stabilization Code (RSC) (9 NYCRR) § 2520.6 (j), since petitioner placed each respondent in occupancy of his respective SRO unit and each respondent “continuously resided” in said unit for more than six months
Respondents’ respective use of the premises cannot be deemed “transient,” inasmuch as they have resided in their units for several years thus qualifying as “permanent tenant[s]”

notes: Six-month statutory threshold is the operative fact; actual tenures ran to several years, which the nights/weeks/months/unclear scale does not capture precisely.

holding_summary: The court upheld the Zoning Board of Appeals' determination that a proposed 16-bed transitional 'sober living' residence for women recovering from substance abuse, where residents pay rent for stays averaging four to nine months, was not a one-family dwelling permitted as of right in a residential district, though it found arbitrary and capricious the further determination that the facility was a 'convalescent home' requiring nursing care.

quotes.text: RSS has not demonstrated that the ZBA’s determination that the proposed residence is not a one-family dwelling is arbitrary and capricious.
